title: An ordinary week, reviewed
hookLine: Yan Hui, one dish of rice in a narrow lane, and a joy hardship couldn't change
tomorrow: why would a teacher point at sheep eating grass?

lines: ONE DISH OF RICE. ONE GOURD.
cards: Scroll back through this week's photos: a parking lot, a bowl of noodles, a receipt you meant to keep. Nothing you'd post. Seven plain days, gone.

Confucius had a student named Yan Hui who lived on less than that. The Analects, the collected sayings of Confucius, picture him with a single bamboo dish of rice, a single gourd of water, living in a narrow little lane.
Others, Confucius says, couldn't have stood it. And then comes the surprising part.

teach.b: He says the hardship never changed Hui's joy. Admirable, he calls him, and says it twice.

teach.h: A BENT ARM FOR A PILLOW.
teach.b: Of himself, in another saying, Confucius says the same: with coarse rice to eat, water to drink, and a bent arm for a pillow, there is still joy in it. Notice what they aren't saying.
They aren't saying poverty is good, or that wanting less will make you feel more.

teach.h: THE JOY IS IN THE WAY.
teach.b: Confucius is honest that the lane was hard. The joy wasn't in the rice. It was in the Way, the life of learning and goodness they were walking, and plain days couldn't reach it.
Later Confucian teachers turned this into a question for their students: find where Confucius and Yan Hui found their joy.
That's the Confucian picture of joy: it lives in how you live, and and it changes how a week looks from Sunday night. A plain week isn't an empty one.
If you were honest, kind and paying attention, through the parking lot and the noodles, it was plain and good.

how: Readers of the Analects return to Yan Hui's narrow lane as a picture of joy in the Way; people who borrow it look back over a plain week and write down what was good in how they lived it.

o: a week with nothing done and nothing to show
seven plain days, looked back on as still good
the five working days, not counting the weekend

games.q: the narrow lane: tap the pairs.
p: one dish of rice, a narrow lane
coarse rice, a bent arm for a pillow
in the Way, not in the rice

s: Confucius taught that being poor is good in itself
the popular misreading. he says others couldn't endure that lane; the joy was in the Way, not the poverty.
Confucius praised Yan Hui because hardship didn't change his joy
he calls Hui admirable, twice, in the same saying.

games.q: your brother calls his week 'nothing': work, gym, frozen dinners. he was honest and kind the whole way through. what fits the Confucian teaching?
o: plain and good: the joy is in how he lived, not in what happened.
a lost week: joy needs something special to happen in it.
it's only good if he cuts back to the bare minimum, like Hui did.
games.why: Yan Hui's joy wasn't in the rice or the lane. it was in the Way he walked, which a plain week can't take away.

practice: Take a pen and something to write on. Look back over the last seven days and write one plain line that was also good, like: Tuesday, soup with a friend. Read it once, then sit with it until the bell.

wordCard.voice: An ordinary week: seven plain days, looked back on the way Confucius looked at Yan Hui's narrow lane.

orig.note: Chinese, from the Analects: he did not change his joy, said of Yan Hui in his narrow lane.

carryVoice: Your line: plain and good. Yan Hui's joy never lived in the rice. That's the week, done.
